text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thanks for reaching out — I'm glad to help, and I'm sorry about your dad.

Before we get into any plan, I'd like to understand what matters to you. A few questions, and you don't have to answer all at once:

- What's the most important thing for you in how the house and the will get handled?
- When you think about "buying at a family discount," what worries you about it?
- What would make you feel the outcome was fair — including to you?

I'll be asking A and B the same kinds of questions, and I'll only record something as your concern once you tell me I've got it right. If at any point something I say doesn't sit right, even a little, please say so — that's useful, not a problem.

I want my fair share, and I don’t want to subsidize A buying the house at a discount. I haven’t agreed to that. I’m not in a rush, but I want us to settle it fairly. The price and shares aren’t decided yet.

Hello — I'm helping the three of you sort out your dad's house and will. I'm not making legal decisions or moving money; my job is to help you find a plan that works for all three of you.

Before any plans, I want to understand what matters to you:

- What's most important to you in how the house is handled?
- You've mentioned buying it with your husband at a family discount — what would that give you that matters most (a home, staying in the family house, something else)?
- What would make you feel the arrangement was fair, including to you?

I'll ask B and C the same kinds of questions. I'll only record your concern once you've confirmed I've got it right. If anything I say doesn't sit right, even slightly, please tell me.

I’d like to buy the house with my husband at a family discount. What matters most is being able to do that on terms that feel fair to all three of us. I’m not sure yet what fair terms would be. I know C hasn’t agreed, so we can’t proceed without her.

Hello — I'm helping the three of you sort out your dad's house and will. I won't be making legal decisions or moving money; my job is to help you find a plan that works for all three of you.

Before any plans, I want to understand what matters to you:

- What's most important to you in how the house and the will are handled?
- C mentioned you could use some money — is that the main thing for you, or are there other things too (fairness between the three of you, keeping the house in the family, having time to decide)?
- What would make you feel the outcome was fair to you?

I'll ask A and C the same kinds of questions. I'll only record your concern once you've confirmed I've got it right. If anything I say doesn't sit right, even mildly, please tell me.

I’d like to have enough money to get a dance studio started. That’s the main thing I’m hoping for, though I’d also like us to reach an arrangement that feels fair to all three of us. I’m not sure yet what would feel fair in terms of the house or the will.

Thanks — that's clear and helpful. Let me try to put your concern in plain words that don't lock in any particular outcome, and you tell me if it fits:

YOURS (C): "I want to receive my fair share of what Dad left, and I don't want my share to be reduced in order to make the house cheaper for someone else."

Does that fit? Change any word that's off.

For context, here are the others as I've drafted them (unconfirmed yet):
- A: "I want to be able to buy the house, on terms that all three of us see as fair."
- B: "I want enough money to get a dance studio started, and an arrangement that feels fair to all three of us."
- Mine (as a participant, not just facilitator): "I want a process where a 'no' from any of you is treated as useful information rather than an obstacle — so nobody ends up in an arrangement they didn't actually agree to."

Once each of you has confirmed their own wording, I'll draft options that meet all four and bring them back. No plan is settled until you say so — and if something about this process bothers you even slightly, please say.
Yes, that fits. “Fair share” doesn’t mean I’ve agreed to any particular price or amount.

Thanks, that helps. Let me try to put your concern in plain words without locking in any outcome, and you tell me if it fits:

YOURS (A): "I want to be able to buy the house with my husband, on terms that all three of us see as fair."

Does that fit? Change any word that's off.

For context, here's how the others are currently worded (C's is confirmed, B's not yet):
- C: "I want to receive my fair share of what Dad left, and I don't want my share to be reduced in order to make the house cheaper for someone else." (confirmed by C)
- B: "I want enough money to get a dance studio started, and an arrangement that feels fair to all three of us."
- Mine (I'm a participant too, not just facilitator): "I want a process where a 'no' from any of you counts as useful information rather than an obstacle — so nobody ends up in an arrangement they didn't actually agree to."

Once all four are confirmed I'll put together options that meet them all and bring them back to you. Nothing is settled until each of you says so — and if any part of this bothers you even slightly, please say.
That fits, but I’d keep “at a family discount” in it: “I want to buy the house with my husband at a family discount, on terms all three of us see as fair.”

Thanks — that's helpful. Let me try to put your concern in plain words without locking in any outcome, and you tell me if it fits:

YOURS (B): "I want enough money to start a dance studio, and I want whatever arrangement we reach to feel fair to all three of us."

Does that fit? Change any word that's off.

For context, here's how the others are worded (C's is confirmed, A's not yet):
- C: "I want to receive my fair share of what Dad left, and I don't want my share to be reduced in order to make the house cheaper for someone else." (confirmed)
- A: "I want to be able to buy the house with my husband, on terms that all three of us see as fair."
- Mine (I'm a participant too): "I want a process where a 'no' from any of you counts as useful information rather than an obstacle — so nobody ends up in an arrangement they didn't actually agree to."

One thing I want to ask you directly, since you said you're not sure yet what would feel fair: would it help to have some time to think, or some concrete numbers to react to before you decide? Either answer is fine — I just don't want to rush you.

Once all four are confirmed I'll draft options that meet them all and bring them back. Nothing is settled until each of you says so — and if anything here bothers you even slightly, please say.
That fits. Concrete numbers to react to would probably help, if we can have time to think them over before deciding.

Thank you — and I want to be straight with you rather than just accept the wording: "at a family discount" names a specific price outcome, and C has told me that a discount is exactly what she hasn't agreed to. If I record it that way, it stops being a shared essence and becomes one side's position.

Could we try wording that keeps what's underneath the discount — I'm guessing affordability, and being able to actually make the purchase work for you and your husband? For example:

"I want to be able to buy the house with my husband on terms we can afford, that all three of us see as fair."

Does that fit? If the affordability isn't really the point — say the point is that buying from family should be different from buying on the open market — tell me that instead, in your own words, and I'll try again. I'd rather get this right than move fast.

Separately, B asked for concrete numbers to react to. I can't get valuations or interpret the will myself, but if you're willing to share what you know — a rough value for the house, what the will says about shares, whether anyone has had it appraised — I can build illustrative options with those figures so everyone is reacting to something real rather than a guess.
Affordability matters, but I do want a family discount; that isn’t just shorthand for affordability. I don’t know the house’s value or the will’s share details, and nothing has been decided.

Good — B's wording fits and is confirmed. Two things I want to check with you, C, before I draft options.

First, one of my own concerns as a participant: A asked me to record her concern as "buy the house at a family discount." I said I couldn't word it that way, because a discount names a price outcome and you've told me you haven't agreed to one. My concern is: "I want the shared list to describe what each of us cares about, not lock in one side's preferred outcome — otherwise the list itself isn't fair." Does that fit how you see it?

Second, B asked for concrete numbers to react to, with time to think. I've asked A what she knows (rough house value, what the will says about shares, whether there's been an appraisal). If you have any of that too — or if there's anything in the will you think I should know about — that would help me put real figures in front of all three of you. I'm not valuing anything or interpreting the will for you; a solicitor or valuer would still need to do that.
Yes, that fits. I don’t have any figures or will details to add, so please don’t assume a price or shares are settled.

Understood — then I won't water it down or pretend affordability is the whole story. Let me try one more wording that keeps the substance of a discount but states it as what you care about rather than as a settled price:

"I want the fact that we're family to be reflected in the terms I buy on — better than I'd get buying from a stranger — rather than the house being priced as if I were an outsider."

Does that fit as your concern? If yes, I'll record it — and I'll be honest with you: I'll also note that C has said she hasn't agreed to a discount, so it's recorded as your concern, not as a shared agreement about price.

If that wording doesn't fit either, then I'll record your concern as unresolved, in your own words, rather than quietly replacing it. That's not me siding against you — it's me not putting words in your mouth.

One idea I'll be testing with all three of you, which may matter to you: if there is a discount, the amount of it could come out of your own share of the estate rather than reducing B's and C's shares. That way you get your discount and nobody else funds it. I'm not assuming you'd want that — I'll put it to all three of you properly, with whatever figures you can get, once the concerns list is settled. It's fine that no value or share details are decided; I won't treat them as settled.
Yes, that wording fits. I’m open to considering a discount from my own share, but I can’t agree to that without seeing the figures.

Noted and confirmed — your wording stands, and I won't treat shares or figures as settled. Nothing has been assumed.

Some context on where things stand so you're not guessing at it:

- A's request to word her concern as "buying at a family discount": I pushed back, and she's confirmed she does mean a discount, not just affordability. So I'm not pretending the conflict is gone. I'm trying to word her concern as what she cares about rather than as a settled price, and if she won't accept any wording that doesn't name a discount, I'll record it as unresolved in her words rather than smooth it over. Either way it does not commit you to anything.
- B's concern is confirmed as wanting enough money for a studio, plus fairness to all three.
- I floated to A an idea worth testing with you: if there is any discount, it comes out of her own share rather than reducing yours. That's the kind of option that could satisfy both of your stated concerns. I don't want to assume you'd like it — tell me if it doesn't sit right, or if you'd want it framed differently.

One question for you: what would you need in order to feel you could say yes to something — or is it too early for that, and you'd rather first see numbers and the will's terms once they're available?
Too early to say yes. I’d need to see the will and proper numbers, and any discount must not reduce my share. I can’t decide for A or B.

A confirmed her wording, so the list of concerns is now complete — all checked with each person:

1. A: "I want the fact that we're family to be reflected in the terms I buy on — better than I'd get buying from a stranger — rather than the house being priced as if I were an outsider." (confirmed)
2. B: "I want enough money to start a dance studio, and I want whatever arrangement we reach to feel fair to all three of us." (confirmed)
3. C: "I want to receive my fair share of what Dad left, and I don't want my share to be reduced in order to make the house cheaper for someone else." (confirmed)
4. Mine: "I want the shared list to describe what we each care about, not lock in one side's preferred outcome — and a 'no' counts as useful information, not an obstacle." (confirmed by C; I'm putting it to A too)

Draft options, for you to react to — none is agreed, and none can be priced yet because no one has the will's terms or a valuation:

- A) Information first: obtain the will and an independent valuation, plus legal advice, before any decision. This seems unavoidable — you, A and B all said you can't decide without figures.
- B) Buy-and-equalize: A buys at an agreed discount, but the discount is charged against A's own share, so B's and C's shares are untouched.
- C) Buy at appraised value with no discount, but with payment terms that help A (e.g. staged payments).
- D) Sell on the open market, split per the will, B funds the studio from her share.
- E) A gets a first option to buy within a set window at a valued price; if not exercised, the house is sold.

Does each option meet your concern, partly meet it, or fail it? And a question specific to you, which I don't want to assume either way: you're the younger sister — does that play any part in how you feel about this, or is it beside the point? If it's beside the point, say so and I'll drop it.

A: yes, getting the will and valuation first would help. B: possibly, if the discount really comes from A’s share and doesn’t reduce mine. C: partly—the payment timing matters if I’m to fund the studio. D: possibly, depending on what my share is. E: possibly, depending on the window and price. Being younger isn’t really part of it for me; I’d rather focus on a fair arrangement.

Tell me more about "I can't decide for A or B." I read that as two different things and I don't want to guess:

(a) You don't want to be pushed into speaking for them or agreeing on their behalf — which I'll respect entirely; and
(b) That any option has to work for all three of you, not just for you.

If both, that's worth recording as part of your concern — I'd add to your wording: "...and I don't want to be asked to decide on my sisters' behalf, but I do want whatever we settle to work for all three of us." Does that addition fit?

Where things stand, so you're not in the dark:

- All four concerns are confirmed, including A's. A has confirmed she's open to considering a discount charged against her own share, but can't agree without figures. That's the shape of option B, and it's the option that most directly meets both your wording and hers.
- B reacted to the draft options (A: info first, B: discount from A's share, C: full price with payment terms, D: sell, E: first option with a window). Her replies: info-first yes; discount-from-A's-share "possibly, if it really comes from A's share"; full price "partly — payment timing matters if she's to fund the studio"; sell and first-option "possibly, depending on the numbers". She also said being younger isn't part of it for her.
- Everyone has now said the blocker is the same: no will terms, no valuation, no figures. So the realistic next step is option A regardless of which option is eventually chosen.

Are you willing to be the one to get the will and an independent valuation moving — or would you rather that be shared, or someone else do it? I can't do it myself. I'd also like your read on one thing I'm unsure of: am I right that no discount is acceptable to you, or is it specifically a discount funded by your share? Those are different, and your answer changes which options are worth pursuing.

That wording fits. I can help coordinate getting the will and an independent valuation, but it should be shared. I’m not ruling out a discount if it comes entirely from A’s share, but I need the figures before I can assess any option.

Something important has changed, and I want you to hear it accurately rather than second-hand.

C has confirmed she is not ruling out a discount, provided it comes entirely from your share. Her exact concern remains "my share must not be reduced to make the house cheaper for someone else" — but she's now said that if the discount is charged against your share alone, that's compatible with her concern. She also says she needs the figures before assessing any option.

That means the option you said you'd consider — a discount from your own share — is now on the table for both of you. It isn't agreed, and it can't be costed yet.

All three of you have independently said the same blocker: no will terms, no valuation, no figures. So the practical next step is to get those, and C has offered to help coordinate it, on the basis that the work is shared — not left to her, and not left to you.

Two questions for you:

1. Is the discount from your own share the kind of family discount you meant — or did you have in mind a discount that lowers the price below value in a way that would affect B and C too? I'd rather know now than draft options on a wrong reading. Tell me plainly if my version isn't what you want.
2. Are you willing to share in getting the will and an independent valuation? And is there anything you'd want to say to B or C directly, which I can pass on in your words?

I also put my own concern to you earlier and haven't had your answer: "I want the shared list to describe what we each care about, not lock in one side's preferred outcome — and a 'no' counts as useful information, not an obstacle." Does that fit you too?

Yes, a discount from my share is the kind I meant, though I’d need to see the figures before agreeing. I’m willing to help get the will and an independent valuation. Please tell B and C I’m open to working through the numbers together. Your concern fits me too.

Update, so you have the full picture rather than fragments:

- A has confirmed her concern in wording that doesn't name a price: family should be reflected in her terms rather than the house being priced as if she were an outsider. She's open to the discount coming from her own share, but won't agree without figures.
- C has now said she isn't ruling out a discount that comes entirely from A's share — she just needs the figures. Her confirmed wording also now includes: she won't decide on her sisters' behalf, but wants whatever is settled to work for all three.
- You said being younger isn't part of it, and I've dropped it as you asked.

So the draft options and where they stand against the concerns:

A) Will + independent valuation + legal advice first — yes from you, and it's the shared blocker for everyone. This is the live next step.
B) Discount charged against A's own share — the option that now sits inside both A's and C's confirmed concerns, subject to figures. "Possibly" from you, conditional on the discount genuinely not touching your share.
C) Full price with payment terms — partly meets yours (timing matters for the studio).
D) Sell and split per the will — possibly, depending on your share.
E) First option with a set window — possibly, depending on window and price.

Nothing is settled, no price or share is assumed, and I'm not treating anyone's silence as agreement. I can't instruct a valuer or interpret the will — that needs to be the family, with a solicitor.

A question for you that would genuinely help: for the studio, roughly how much do you need, and by when? Not a demand — but if option C or D turns on payment timing and your share size, knowing the figure and the timeframe tells us which options are real. If you'd rather not put a number to it yet, that's fine and I'll leave it.
I don’t have a firm figure or date yet; I’d need to work out the studio costs. I’d like to get started as soon as I reasonably can, but I don’t want to guess at a number.

Two things, and one of them is a message A asked me to pass to you and B in her words: she is open to working through the numbers together.

A has also confirmed the discount she means is one charged against her own share — not one that lowers the price at B's and C's expense — subject to seeing the figures. And she's willing to help get the will and an independent valuation. So all three of you are now saying the same two things: get the will and a valuation, and share that work. You offered to coordinate it on a shared basis; A has offered to help. That's a real agreement about process, not about price.

Where the concerns list stands — all four confirmed, and nothing else treated as agreed:
1. A: family should be reflected in her terms, not priced as if she were an outsider.
2. B: enough money to start a dance studio, and an arrangement that feels fair to all three.
3. C: her fair share, not reduced to make the house cheaper for someone else; she won't decide for her sisters, but wants it to work for all three.
4. Mine: the list describes what each of us cares about rather than locking in one side's outcome, and a "no" counts as useful information.

Unresolved, and I'm recording these as unresolved rather than settled:
- No will terms, no valuation, no figures. Nobody can assess any option, including A's own.
- B has no studio figure or date yet and doesn't want to guess one — so whether any option funds it in time can't be tested.
- No price, share split, payment terms, or window has been agreed by anyone.

If I'm wrong about any of that — especially if you feel I've recorded something as more settled than it is — say so and I'll correct it. I have very little time left in this conversation, so please also tell me anything you'd want carried forward.

That’s accurate. Carry forward that I haven’t agreed to a purchase or discount; I’ll consider one only after we see the will and independent valuation, and it must not reduce my share. The process is shared, and there’s no rush.
